chapter: Learning violin and banjo in New Orleans
title: Violin method with Dave Perkins and picking up banjo with Morris and Mack
summary: Perkins starts him on rudiments and the fingerboard for three years; his brother's banjo leads him to read and fake with George Morris and others, and he graduates eighth grade.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: About how old were you? Can we get that?

Well, it's kind of hard. I should have figured it out, but I was in about fourth or fifth grade. Well, you're quite young. At that time, kids were pretty old. I mean, not like now, you know, so I must have been around about 10 or 11 years old, maybe older than that. Because I can wait and bring in this park. I can remember in 1924, I was just about ready to make it. I hadn't quite, I hadn't even made 18 or close to it. And that was April, like I'm born in January. And that was when, of course, I'm going to get to that. So you can subtract from that. So we will get to that. Talking at that time. I can't remember how old I was at that time. I'm taking lessons. So that's when I went to Mr. Dave Poick, and I had this big viola. So he says, Noah, you got, I had bought my book. And it was one of those outdoor language books there. That was all the books he taught all his college that went there. If you, whatever instrument you played, you had to get an outdoor language method of a drum, or a clandlet, or whatever it was. And they were very good methods. And he said, Noah, you don't need this instrument now. He said, you're going to spend a little time on just learning the rudiments of music, and your signs, and different things. And I stayed about, I stayed over a month, just with the method. Just learning how the staff, and the lines, and then learning the notes, and the value of the notes, and learning the different signs, you know, and the music, you know, like your piano missile, and 40 missile, whatever those were signed, all those. And I used to have to memorize that whole sheet. Of course, at that time, I was a pretty good guy in school. I mean, I had a pretty good little schooling, you know. And after I say about four or six weeks, and he let me brought the instrument around, and he took me on the diagram of the fingerboard. And he gave me a little, uh, parts to go on that, to learn parts of the fingerboard. And the next time I learned about it, the next time he stopped me on how to handle the bow, and how to, how to, you know, hold your bow, and how to hold the violin and everything. Well, to put it short, I studied the violin with him, I believe, about, about three years, so. And, uh, my brother Pete was working down at Whirline's store, and he used to bring a lot of music, you know. And, uh, in taking a lesson, I used to always be warned the professor Dave when I'm going to start playing some songs, you know. But he didn't know I hadn't, after I had learned my skills and things, I had some piano schools, I was already playing some songs already, just, you know. So, uh, then, uh, the banjo came out. No, it was already out, but I mean, it became very popular. My brother Pete had bought a banjo, and he thought he wanted to learn, so he said, well, you can teach me, so you, you know, about me, so I want to learn how to read. So I was teaching him everything, and, but, uh, Pete didn't get so interested in it then, so I, by teaching him, I was learning myself. So, uh, I thought that, uh, there's some fellas named George Morris, and a fella named George, Mac, was taking the last one by in Puick, and they had a little banjo, you see, and they was having trouble with the guy playing the banjo, because they could read and also fake, you see, because I couldn't fake so much, but I could, I could read then, so they said, well, how about I come around out of rehearsal and bring your banjo, and said, we got music here, so we know you can read. So they found out that I could fit in pretty good, and by playing with them, that's how I learned how to fake, you see. So I was to take my lesson from, from Puykin, and, uh, I remember I had, uh, I had finished eighth grade, I had graduated at, uh, at, uh, at Tom LaFont School, and, uh, I remember the teacher up there, Mrs. Cornelia, she wasn't the principal, but she was a popular teacher up there, and she, in our classes, we had one of the largest eighth grade classes that ever graduated at that time, we had three eighth grade classes, and, uh, she had requested that we would hire Willie Hump.
